extracted.intended_audience: students, educators, and general readers interested in humour research, self-assessment, and personality correlates
extracted.subtask_description: Summarise and classify individual differences in humour via the Humour Styles Questionnaire (HSQ), describing four humour styles, their outcomes, personality correlates, and measurement properties. Useful for researchers, educators, or practitioners wanting to assess or understand how people use humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affiliative Humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Affiliative humour is used to enhance your relationships with others in a kind and benevolent way. People who regularly demonstrate affiliative humour will amuse and charm others and ease tensions in challenging situations. Affiliative humour is often spontaneous, utilising joke telling and witty banter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People high in affiliative humour tend to share humour with others, tell jokes and funny stories, amuse others, make others laugh and enjoy laughing along with others. Outcomes: improved social intimacy; more likely to initiate friendships; support group cohesion; promote creativity in self and others; decreased anxiety; improved self-esteem; improved psychological well-being. Personality correlates: higher extraversion and openness to experience. Similarities/differences: shares intent to enhance relationships with self-defeating humour (but without self-cost); shares benign intent with self-enhancing humour (but more relationship-focused). Example HSQ items: "I rarely make other people laugh by telling funny stories about myself" (reverse scored). "I don’t often joke around with my friends" (reverse scored).

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-Enhancing Humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-enhancing humour is used in a benign way to enhance the individual using humour. Someone using self-enhancing humour would laugh at their own failings and situations in a constructive, non-defeating manner; it functions as an emotional regulator or coping strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People high in self-enhancing humour maintain a humorous outlook even when alone, use humour to cope with stress, and cheer themselves up. Outcomes: less likely to exhibit depressive symptoms; improved psychological well-being; increased creativity; reduced stress and anxiety; improved self-esteem and optimism. Personality correlates: higher extraversion and openness, lower neuroticism. Similarities/differences: shares benign intent with affiliative humour but is more self-focused; shares self-enhancement intent with aggressive humour but is benevolent rather than injurious. Example HSQ items: "If I am feeling upset or unhappy I usually try to think of something funny about the situation to make myself feel better." "Even when I’m by myself, I’m often amused by the absurdities of life."

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggressive Humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggressive humour is a humour style typically detrimental to others, including put-downs, teasing, sarcasm, ridicule and other humour used at the expense of others. It often shows little consideration for the impact on others and can be hostile in intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People high in aggressive humour tend to use humour to disparage, put down, or manipulate others; employ ridicule, offensive humour, or compulsive joking even when inappropriate. Outcomes: higher hostility and aggression; less likely to initiate relationships; reduced creativity in self and others; reduced group cohesion. Personality correlates: higher neuroticism, lower agreeableness and conscientiousness; males more likely to use aggressive humour. Similarities/differences: shares self-enhancement intent with self-enhancing humour but differs in injurious/hostile intent; shares injurious aspects with self-defeating humour but differs in target (others vs self). Example HSQ items: "When telling jokes or saying funny things, I am usually not very concerned about how other people are taking it." "People are never offended or hurt by my sense of humour" (reverse scored).

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-Defeating Humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-defeating humour is used to enhance relationships and gain approval from others by making oneself the butt of the joke; it is detrimental to the person using the humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People high in self-defeating humour engage in self-disparaging humour, laughing at themselves or at their own expense; may use it as a defence mechanism or to avoid dealing with negative feelings. Outcomes: higher levels of depression and anxiety; reduced self-esteem and psychological well-being; reduced social intimacy. Personality correlates: higher neuroticism, lower agreeableness and conscientiousness. Similarities/differences: shares relationship-enhancing intent with affiliative humour but is injurious to self; shares injurious aspects with aggressive humour but differs in target (self vs others). Example HSQ items: "If I am having problems or feeling unhappy, I often cover it up by joking around, so that even my closest friends don’t know how I really feel." "I often try to make people like or accept me more by saying something funny about my own weaknesses, blunders, or faults."

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour Styles Questionnaire (HSQ) measurement structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The HSQ is a 32-item self-report inventory (Martin et al., 2003) that identifies how a person uses humour in everyday life. Participants respond on a 7-point scale (ranging from totally agree to totally disagree).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The questionnaire measures humour against two main factors: (1) whether humour is used to enhance the self or enhance relationships with others, and (2) whether the humour is benign or detrimental to others or self; the combination creates a 2x2 matrix of four humour styles (Affiliative, Self-Enhancing, Aggressive, Self-Defeating). Some HSQ items are reverse-scored. Reliability notes: original German version reported internal consistency (alpha) > 0.77 for all scales; translation studies show variation — Taher et al. (2008) reported alpha from 0.55 (aggressive) to 0.89 (self-enhancing); Bilge & Saltuk (2007) reported 0.67 (self-defeating) to 0.78 (self-enhancing). The aggressive scale often produces the lowest internal consistency. Translation can produce more varied items and affect reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matrix axes for classifying humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Two orthogonal dimensions are used to classify humour styles: (A) enhancing the self vs enhancing relationships with others, and (B) benign (non-injurious) vs injurious (detrimental) intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The intersection of these axes produces the four humour styles: Affiliative (enhance relationships; benign), Self-Enhancing (enhance self; benign), Aggressive (enhance self; injurious), Self-Defeating (enhance relationships; injurious). The matrix is the conceptual rubric for interpreting HSQ scores and for reasoning about the social/psychological consequences of humour use.
